title: Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity)
subject: psychiatry
summary: Diagnose clinically with the Hunter criteria (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor with agitation or sweating), stop all serotonergic drugs and give benzodiazepines with supportive care. Cyproheptadine 12 mg then 2 mg every 2 hours may help moderate cases; severe hyperthermia with rigidity needs rapid cooling, paralysis and ventilation.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Triad: neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (sweating, tachycardia, hyperthermia, mydriasis, diarrhoea) and altered mental state (anxiety, agitation, confusion).
Develops rapidly, usually within hours of starting, increasing or combining serotonergic drugs, or after overdose.
Common causes: SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs (including linezolid and methylene blue), clomipramine and other TCAs, tramadol, pethidine, fentanyl, dextromethorphan, lithium and MDMA.
Highest risk: an MAOI combined with an SSRI or another serotonergic drug; almost half of such overdoses develop toxicity, often severe.
Life-threatening toxicity: rapidly rising temperature above 40°C with increasing (especially truncal) rigidity that impairs breathing.

sections.title: Diagnosis (Hunter criteria)
items: Hunter criteria, in a patient on a serotonergic drug, any one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or sweating; ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; tremor with hyperreflexia; hypertonia with temperature above 38°C and ocular or inducible clonus.
Clonus and hyperreflexia are usually more marked in the lower limbs.
No confirmatory test. Check CK, creatinine, electrolytes, blood gas, glucose and coagulation (DIC in severe cases).
Exclude sepsis, meningitis or encephalitis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, anticholinergic or sympathomimetic toxicity, alcohol withdrawal and heat stroke.
NMS differs: onset over days after a dopamine antagonist, lead-pipe rigidity and slow (bradyreflexic) responses rather than clonus.

sections.title: Mild to moderate toxicity
items: Stop all serotonergic drugs and avoid adding new ones. Mild toxicity usually resolves within 24 hours.
Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen, cardiac monitoring. Avoid physical restraint, which increases muscle activity, heat and lactic acidosis.
Benzodiazepines for agitation, tremor and muscle activity: for example diazepam 5 to 10 mg orally or IV, or lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV, repeated as needed.

Cyproheptadine (oral or crushed via nasogastric tube) may give symptomatic relief in moderate toxicity: 12 mg initially, then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptoms continue; maintenance 8 mg every 6 hours. Evidence is weak.
Chlorpromazine IM or IV (doses of 12.5 to 100 mg reported) is a parenteral 5-HT2A antagonist alternative with limited evidence; it can cause hypotension and should be avoided if NMS is possible.

sections.title: Severe toxicity
items: Treat in ICU. The priority is aggressive supportive care, not an antidote.
Active rapid cooling (ice packs, evaporative cooling, cooling blankets, ice-water immersion). Antipyretics such as paracetamol do not help because the heat comes from muscle activity.

Temperature above 39°C with agitation, altered consciousness or rigidity, or not responding to cooling: early sedation, intubation and non-depolarising neuromuscular paralysis. Avoid suxamethonium (hyperkalaemia with rhabdomyolysis).
Hypertension and tachycardia usually settle with sedation; use short-acting agents if treatment is needed. Hypotension: fluids, then a direct-acting vasopressor (noradrenaline).
Dantrolene and bromocriptine have no role in serotonin toxicity.

sections.title: Monitoring and disposition
items: Monitor core temperature, clonus and rigidity, heart rate and BP; check CK, creatinine and potassium for rhabdomyolysis; watch for seizures and DIC.
Long half-life drugs (fluoxetine) or MAOIs can prolong toxicity and interactions for days to weeks after stopping.
Before discharge, review the whole medication list, document the interaction, and delay restarting serotonergic drugs until toxicity has fully resolved.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Relying on cyproheptadine in severe hyperthermia instead of cooling, paralysis and ventilation.
Physical restraint of an agitated, hyperthermic patient.
Adding linezolid, methylene blue, tramadol or pethidine to a patient on an SSRI or MAOI.
Confusing serotonin toxicity with NMS or sepsis and giving an antipsychotic or dantrolene.

drugs.name: Cyproheptadine
drugs.dose: 12 mg orally or via nasogastric tube, then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptomatic; maintenance 8 mg every 6 hours
drugs.notes: Oral only; sedating; weak evidence; not a substitute for supportive care.

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: 5 to 10 mg orally or IV, repeat as needed

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 mg IV, repeat as needed

drugs.name: Chlorpromazine
drugs.dose: 12.5 to 100 mg IM or slow IV (reported range)
drugs.notes: Limited evidence; hypotension; avoid if NMS possible.

algorithms.title: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria Decision Tree

steps.action: Confirm therapeutic exposure, dose escalation, or overdose with a serotonergic drug (SSRI, SNRI, MAOI, tramadol, linezolid).
Definitive Serotonin Toxicity confirmed. Discontinue all serotonergic agents immediately and start supportive care.
Meets Hunter criteria for Serotonin Toxicity. Administer IV benzodiazepines (diazepam or lorazepam) for neuromuscular hyperactivity.
Meets Hunter criteria for Serotonin Toxicity. Monitor core temperature and start aggressive cooling if > 38.5 C.
Meets Hunter criteria for Serotonin Toxicity. Start oral cyproheptadine 12 mg if mild to moderate and supportive care is insufficient.
Severe life-threatening toxicity. Immediate endotracheal intubation, neuromuscular paralysis with vecuronium or rocuronium, and ICU admission. Never use succinylcholine.
